# Purpose of This Document

This is a management summary, not a specification. It reports whether the
S5/b testing-mode implementation actually behaves as `technology/consensus-transition.md`
and `analysis/Rincoin_840k_S5B_Consensus_Change_Specification.qmd` say it
should — checked by running it, not by re-reading the design. The full
evidence — every test case, raw logs, exact commits — is in
[`S5B/`](S5B/), not repeated here.

This scenario's testing-mode branch was built by branching directly from
the already-tested `consensus/s1-testing` branch and reusing its shared
infrastructure (coinbase commitment, `sig_fork_id`, mainnet blocker, wallet/
PSBT signing) unmodified — confirmed scenario-agnostic by direct code
review before branching, not assumed. Only the subsidy formula and a
handful of identity constants changed. This document's structure mirrors
[S1's own summary](S1_Consensus_Testing_Summary.qmd) directly, not as a
separate design exercise.

# What Changes at H1, Briefly

At block height 840,000 (mainnet), three things change together: the block
subsidy schedule, a scheduled coinbase commitment identifying the chosen
schedule, and a sighash-level replay identifier (`sig_fork_id`) mixed into
new transaction signatures. The commitment and `sig_fork_id` mechanisms are
identical across every candidate scenario; only the subsidy schedule
differs. S5/b's schedule: an extended, 10x-longer halving epoch,
phase-anchored to height 840,000 − `nSubsidyHalvingInterval` (630,000 on
mainnet — the pre-activation epoch boundary, *not* the activation height
itself), then plain binary halving per extended epoch, no floor, no tail.
Full rationale and byte-level specification:
`analysis/Rincoin_840k_S5B_Consensus_Change_Specification.qmd`. This
document assumes that design and tests it; it does not re-argue it.

# Summary

**Every test that has been run passes.** 532 of 532 C++ unit tests, 159 of
159 functional tests (the fork-specific suite plus the full pre-existing CI
allowlist, unmodified), and every cross-implementation comparison run so
far. One real defect in the *test suite itself* (not the consensus
implementation) was found and fixed while adapting it for this scenario's
structurally different epoch length — reported in Results as part of the
evidence, not as a caveat against it.

{{< include includes/s5b_results_summary_table.qmd >}}

Two evidence layers are not yet complete, both inherited from S1 rather
than newly discovered here: the full cross-implementation producer ×
validator matrix, and two narrow commitment test-vector cases. Neither is
scenario-specific — closing them once closes them for S1, S5/b, and S6/b
together. See Results §5.4 and [`S5B/open-items.md`](S5B/open-items.md).

Read **Methods** below for what "tested" means in each row above and why it
was tested that way; read **Results** for the detail behind each pass.

# Methods: What Was Tested, and How

Four groups, used consistently through both this section and Results — the
same four used for S1, since the mechanism being tested is identical:

| Group | What it checks | Why it's a separate group |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit-level | Each piece of consensus logic (subsidy formula, commitment parsing, sighash mixing) against frozen, byte-exact vectors | Smallest testable unit; catches an error before it can reach anything that depends on it |
| Single-node functional | The same rules, enforced end-to-end by a real running node via RPC/P2P | Unit tests exercise logic in-process; this confirms the rules hold when driven the way a real deployment would drive them |
| Multi-node functional | Whether the network prefers higher work only when that chain is also rule-valid | This is the entire reason the coinbase-commitment mechanism exists — it has to be checked directly, not inferred from the rule existing |
| Cross-implementation | What happens when this build meets software that disagrees with it | The only layer that reflects the network as it actually is, not just this codebase |

## Unit-level

The subsidy formula is checked against frozen vectors from two independent
sources agreeing: `analysis/data/S5B_normative_test_vectors.csv` (the file
the specification itself names as the conformance target) and a
from-scratch Python re-derivation of the published formula
(`verification/scripts/independently_derive_s5b_schedule.py`) that does not
import the C++ implementation. The commitment builder/parser and
`sig_fork_id` sighash-mixing code are reused unmodified from
`consensus/s1-testing` — their own tests already check them against
frozen vectors independent of which subsidy scenario is compiled in.

Every pre-existing sighash and script unit test in the codebase is also
re-run, unmodified, as a no-regression guard.

## Single-node functional

Driven through a real, running `rincoind` process via its actual RPC and
P2P interfaces, not exercised in-process: coinbase-commitment validation
(reused unmodified from S1 — the malformation catalog doesn't depend on the
subsidy scenario), and subsidy enforcement both at H1 and at the real
second phase boundary (H1 + 9 halving-intervals for this scenario, not one
— see the Results note on why this needed a real fix, not just a constant
change).

## Multi-node functional

Two testing-mode nodes, connected and synced past the activation height,
one isolated and used to mine two competing continuations: a longer chain
that is also commitment-valid, and a longer chain that is
commitment-*invalid*. Both chains are offered back to the network; which
one is adopted is the entire test. Reused unmodified from S1 — this
mechanism doesn't depend on the subsidy scenario either.

## Cross-implementation

Every accessible node binary — this implementation, older Rincoin releases,
and independently developed forks reachable on a shared network — tested as
both block *producer* and block *validator* against every other binary.

::: {.callout-note}

# Results: Did It Pass?

## Unit-level — pass

532 of 532 C++ unit tests pass (one unrelated, pre-existing warning, same
as S1's own report). The subsidy schedule's two independent sources agree
with each other and with the C++ implementation at every height checked:

{{< include includes/s5b_vector_spotcheck_table.qmd >}}

The commitment-parsing vector catalog carries the same two open exceptions
S1's own annex tracks (not new to this scenario): see
[`S5B/commitment-test-vectors.md`](S5B/commitment-test-vectors.md).

Full detail and reproduction commands: [`S5B/unit-test-results.md`](S5B/unit-test-results.md).

## Single-node functional — pass

All commitment-validation and subsidy-enforcement checks pass against a
real running node. One genuine test-suite defect was found and fixed here,
not in the implementation under test: the inherited "next epoch boundary"
check assumed the wrong offset for this scenario's 10x-longer post-fork
epoch, which (once corrected to the real offset) crossed the regtest MWEB
activation height and exposed that hand-built test blocks can't satisfy
MWEB's extension-block requirement. Fixed with a scenario-portable offset
constant and a real-miner-based fallback check past MWEB activation — full
account in [`S5B/unit-test-results.md`](S5B/unit-test-results.md) and
[`S5B/functional-test-results.md`](S5B/functional-test-results.md).

## Multi-node functional — pass

Both reorg outcomes are correct, reusing S1's own mechanism test unmodified:
the higher-work, commitment-*valid* chain is adopted; the higher-work,
commitment-*invalid* chain is not.

## Cross-implementation — partially done, passing so far

The full producer × validator matrix has not been run. The two narrower
comparisons that are done both pass for what they cover, with the same
conclusions already established for S1 (this mechanism doesn't depend on
the subsidy scenario): S5/b vs. `v1.1.0` diverges cleanly at the activation
height; S5/b vs. `v1.0.1` diverges with no crash; S5/b vs. the foreign
`Aevust/rincoin` fork shows the header/full-block asymmetry the mechanism
is designed to produce (best-known-header can advance, validated tip does
not). Full detail: [`S5B/functional-test-results.md`](S5B/functional-test-results.md).

# Scope: What This Testing Does Not Cover

Same deliberate scoping as S1 — not repeated in full here since none of it
is scenario-specific. See
[S1's own "Scope" section](S1_Consensus_Testing_Summary.qmd) for the full
reasoning: header-level branch isolation, a dedicated P2P
branch-declaration message, staged release engineering, live mainnet
telemetry, and pool/seeder integration rehearsals are all out of scope or
outstanding for the same reasons there.
